## Two claims about the world

A spatial lag says that a neighbour's *outcome* moves yours: a tax rate
set with an eye on the next state's, a disease that spreads, a price that
buyers compare across a border. A spatial error says that only the
*shocks* are shared: the weather that hits a whole valley, a
measurement error that is local, a variable the model left out that
happens to cluster on the map. The first is a mechanism; the second is a
nuisance that has to be allowed for, or, as @holly2010 read it for
house prices, the diffusion of a shock that is itself worth measuring
[@croissant2019, sec. 10.2.2]. They are not two ways to fit one curve.
They are different statements about what would happen if one unit's
outcome were changed, and the [effects
note](theory-direct-indirect-effects.qmd) spells out the difference.

## 1. The specifications

Stack the N units of period *t* [@pesaran2015, eqs. 30.1–30.9;
@baltagi2021, pp. 401–406]:

| Name | Equation | Claim |
|---|---|---|
| **SAR**, spatial lag | $y_t = \rho W y_t + X_t\beta + u_t$ | outcomes move outcomes |
| **SEM**, spatial error | $y_t = X_t\beta + u_t,\ u_t = \lambda W u_t + \varepsilon_t$ | shocks are shared |
| **SARAR** | both, with $W_1$ and $W_2$ possibly different | both |
| **SDM**, Durbin | $y_t = \rho W y_t + X_t\beta + W X_t\theta + u_t$ | neighbours' regressors matter too |

The reduced forms say what each does to an estimate. Under SAR,
$y_t = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X_t\beta + u_t)$: $Wy_t$ contains $u_t$ and is
endogenous, so least squares on it, pooled or within, is inconsistent
[@pesaran2015, p. 800; @baltagi2021, p. 401]. Under SEM,
$u_t = (I - \lambda W)^{-1}\varepsilon_t$: the regressors stay exogenous,
and least squares is consistent and merely inefficient, with standard
errors that are wrong. @pesaran2015 [p. 801] put the consequence in one
line: under spatial *errors*, fixed and random effects are
$\sqrt{NT}$-consistent, and spatial modelling buys efficiency, not
consistency.

The Durbin term $WX_t$ costs nothing in estimation: $WX_t$ is as
exogenous as $X_t$, and `splm::slag()` adds it to any formula. What it
changes is the reading of the coefficients, since the effect of $x_k$ on
unit *i* now runs through $\beta_k$ and $\theta_k$ together
[@baltagi2021, p. 406; @lesage2009, sec. 2.7].

## 2. The Lagrange multiplier battery

The tests of @anselin1996 need only the non-spatial fit. With residuals
*e*, the error test is

$$
LM_\lambda = \frac{(e'We/\hat\sigma^2)^2}{T_W}, \qquad
T_W = \operatorname{tr}(W'W + W^2),
$$

and the lag test replaces $e'We$ with $e'Wy$ and $T_W$ with a term that
also involves the fitted values. Each is $\chi^2_1$ under its null, and
each rejects under the *other's* alternative, because an omitted lag
leaves spatially correlated residuals and an omitted error makes $Wy$
look informative. The **robust** versions subtract from each statistic
the part the other effect would contribute [@anselin1996, eqs. 10, 13]:

$$
RLM_\lambda =
  \frac{\big(e'We/\hat\sigma^2 - T_W\, \tilde J^{-1}\, e'Wy/\hat\sigma^2\big)^2}
       {T_W\,(1 - T_W \tilde J^{-1})},
$$

with $\tilde J$ the information term of the lag test. The adjustment is
exact for a *local* departure, a small value of the other parameter, and
"can behave suboptimally" when both effects are large [@croissant2019,
sec. 10.3.4.2]. The reading rule that follows is in two parts. When a
plain test rejects and its robust version does not, the signal was the
other effect's shadow, which is the rice case: `lml` = 39, `rlml` = 0.17.
When both robust tests reject strongly, the tests have left their design
range, which is the house-price case: `rlml` = 32, `rlme` = 28. The answer
then comes from the fits.

`slmtest` implements the four for a *pooled* model, which is what
@anselin1996 derived. With unit effects, pass `model = "within"` or
demean the variables with `plm::Within()` in the formula; the
[lag-or-error section](index.qmd#sec-sp-lag-or-error) does both.

## 3. The encompassing model as arbiter

When the robust tests do not settle it, fit SARAR and read it two ways
[@croissant2019, sec. 10.3.4.2]. A **Wald** *z* on each spatial parameter
needs no robustification, since the other effect is in the model. A
**likelihood ratio** between SARAR and the nested SAR or SEM,
$2[\ln L_{\text{SARAR}} - \ln L_{\text{SEM}}] \sim \chi^2_1$, asks whether
the lag adds anything given the error, and the reverse. On rice with
random effects the lag given the error has p = 0.91: the error is the
whole story.

The arbiter has one weakness. With the *same* W in both places, a SARAR
model is close to unidentified: a positive error and a negative lag can
reproduce the covariance of a plain SEM, and the two parameters trade off
against each other with large standard errors [@elhorst2014, ch. 2;
@lesage2009, ch. 2]. The transformed house-price panel shows it, with a
lag of −0.52 and an error of 0.87 where the separate fits gave 0.65 and
0.69. In that case the encompassing model reports two numbers that mean
less than either separate one, and the honest write-up gives SEM and SAR
side by side with their impacts.

## 4. The unit effect's own spatial structure

With random effects there is a further choice [@baltagi2021, pp. 393–395;
@pesaran2015, p. 803]. In Anselin's specification the unit effect is
plain and only the period shock passes through $(I - \lambda W)^{-1}$;
the spillovers are time-varying. In the specification of @kapoor2007
the unit effect passes through it too, so a good farmer raises the
neighbours' output in every season; the spillovers are time-invariant as
well. @baltagi2013 nest both in a model with three matrices. The two
differ only through the variance ratio of the unit effect; when it is
small, as on rice, the fits are the same to the second decimal, and the
[random-effects section](index.qmd#sec-sp-re) shows it. Whether the unit
effect may be random at all is the spatial Hausman test's question, and
its answer depends on the spatial model it is asked under: on rice it
rejects under the error model and not under the lag model.

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| The question is a mechanism, outcomes moving outcomes | SAR or SDM, and report impacts, not β |
| The question is a slope, with shocks that cluster | SEM; β is the effect, and the fit buys precision |
| Plain lag test rejects, robust lag test does not | The lag was the error's shadow; SEM |
| Both robust tests reject strongly | Fit SEM, SAR and SARAR; if SARAR's parameters flip sign, report the two separate fits |
| Neighbours' regressors plausibly matter | Add $WX$ with `splm::slag()`; the effects change, the estimation does not |
| Unit effects are random and large | Anselin against KKP matters; with a small variance ratio it does not |
| A shock should stop at the first neighbour | The error form needed is not implemented; state it |

## Open

- **SMA and SEC errors** [@pesaran2015, eqs. 30.5–30.6] are not in
  **splm**, which fits the autoregressive error only.
- **The fixed-effects LM and LR tests of @debarsy2010**, joint, marginal
  and conditional, are not implemented; their LR *structure* can be
  rebuilt from the log-likelihoods of nested `spml` fits, but the within
  log-likelihoods of **splm** are not on one scale across lag and error
  fits, so the comparison has to run with random effects.
- **A test for the Durbin term** beyond the Wald *z* on $\theta$ is not
  covered here.
